title: Evaluating the effectiveness of copper sulphate, chlorine, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide and ozone on cyanobacterial cell integrity
authors: Fan J, Ho L, Hobson P, Brookes J
scale: bench cultures of toxic M. aeruginosa strain 338 in ASM-1, initial 7.0 x 10^5 cells/mL, triplicate
dose: CuSO4 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 mg/L as Cu; chlorine 3, 4, 5 mg/L; KMnO4 1, 3, 5, 10 mg/L; H2O2 10.2, 51, 102 mg/L; ozone 2, 4, 6 mg/L
result: All five treatments compromised membranes (flow cytometry, SYTOX Green): chlorine >=88% of cells within 1 min, ozone 6 mg/L 90% in 5 min, KMnO4 10 mg/L no intact cells after 6 h. Cell densities fell much less: about 22% after 3 days with 1.0-1.5 mg/L Cu, about 15% with 10 mg/L KMnO4, and no significant change with ozone or H2O2.
env_effects: All oxidants compromise cell membranes, so intracellular metabolites (toxins, taste and odour compounds) are released; fast lysers release them at once.
key_details: Lab time-course experiments on a toxic Microcystis aeruginosa strain (7.0 x 10^5 cells/mL, 20 C, pH 7.5) with untreated controls; triplicate analyses. The endpoint is membrane integrity by flow cytometry, not cell removal. CuSO4 1.5 mg/L gave >95% compromised cells; with 1.0 mg/L 98% were impaired at day 2 but intact cells rose again after day 3. H2O2 left 16%, 31% and 7% intact on day 2 at 10.2, 51 and 102 mg/L, yet 82% were viable again by day 7 at 51 mg/L and densities did not differ significantly from controls. Ozone 2, 4, 6 mg/L compromised about 50%, 70% and 90% of cells in 5 min with no significant density change.
fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct 90 was the ozone membrane-compromise percentage, not a reduction in algae; cell densities barely changed for ozone and H2O2 (at most ~22% drop with CuSO4). The H2O2 'algistatic' claim is weak: cells recovered integrity after day 3 and densities did not differ from controls.

title: Comparison of permanganate preoxidation and preozonation on algae containing water: cell integrity, characteristics, and chlorinated disinfection byproduct formation
authors: Xie P, Ma J, Fang J, Guan Y, Yue S, Li X, Chen L
scale: bench suspensions of M. aeruginosa (1.01 x 10^6 cells/mL, TOC 5 mg/L) in simulated drinking water, duplicate tests
dose: KMnO4 or ozone 0-2.0 mg/L preoxidation (10 min, pH 7.0), then coagulation-sedimentation or chlorination (Cl2:TOC 3:1, 3 days)
result: Preozonation at 0.4-2.0 mg/L left <=1% intact cells, while permanganate 0.4-2.0 mg/L kept >97% live cells. Both preoxidants raised cell removal by coagulation-sedimentation from 56.7% to 78.0% (KMnO4 1.0 mg/L) and 80.2% (ozone 2.0 mg/L).
env_effects: Preozonation released intracellular organic matter and dramatically increased chlorinated disinfection by-products (haloaldehydes, haloacetonitriles, halonitromethanes); permanganate had much less effect. Authors favour permanganate over ozone.
key_details: Bench study in simulated drinking water (pH 7.0, 25 C) with M. aeruginosa washed free of extracellular organic matter; tests in duplicate with an unoxidized control. Endpoints were flow-cytometric cell integrity, coagulation removal, DOC and 3-day chlorination by-products. Ozone raised DOC after coagulation from 0.42 to 1.00 mg/L; permanganate left DOC unchanged. Common DBPs (TCM, DCAA, TCAA) rose >40% at 2.0 mg/L ozone, CH and TCNM by 262% and 471%; permanganate changed most DBPs only slightly. Removal gains levelled off above 1.0 mg/L oxidant.
fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct 98 was the share of cells lysed by ozone (not removal); the actual removal endpoint is coagulation-sedimentation removal, 80.2% with ozone vs 56.7% without preoxidation.

title: Effectiveness of ozone nanobubble treatments on high biomass cyanobacterial blooms: A mesocosm experiment and field trial
authors: Chaffin JD, Berthold DE, Braig EC, Fuchs JD, Gabor RS, Jacquemin SJ, et al.
organism: Planktothrix (cyanobacteria bloom), Grand Lake St Marys, Ohio
scale: 2,000 L mesocosms plus two 4-week trials in a ~4.7e7 L lake embayment
dose: Mesocosm applied ozone 4.8 +/- 0.6, 7.1 +/- 0.8 and 15 +/- 1 mg O3/L (O3:DOC 0.68, 1.21, 2.04; DOC ~7.2 mg C/L), plus oxygen-only nanobubble control; field: two NBOT units in a 3.2 x 10^4 m2, ~1.5 m deep embayment (4.8 x 10^4 m3) at lower O3:DOC
result: In 2,000 L mesocosms (3 tanks per dose, 100% of water passed through the unit) medium and high doses cut chl-a and phycocyanin 98-99% and microcystins 62% and 92%; low dose cut chl-a >70%. In the embayment trials there was no effect: chl-a at the outlet and 3.3 m away was within +/-10% of the inlet except one sample (-34.3%).
env_effects: DOC was more oxidized at the outlet; treatment reach minimal. Failure attributed to high biomass and DOC, low O3:DOC and small fraction of lake water treated.
key_details: Replicated mesocosm (triplicate tanks per dose, untreated and oxygen-only controls, sampled 1-96 h) plus two 4-week field deployments in the Sunset Beach embayment of Grand Lake St Marys, Ohio. The mesocosm bloom was diluted with 60% filtered Lake Erie water, so starting biomass was lower than in the lake, flattering the mesocosm result. Oxygen-only nanobubbles had no effect. Field failure attributed to high biomass and DOC, O3:DOC below the lowest mesocosm dose, and only a small fraction of lake water treated at any time; SUVA254 showed ozone reacted only near the outlet.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record is accurate; it omits that the mesocosm water was diluted 60% with filtered Lake Erie water, and the absolute ozone doses (4.8-15 mg O3/L).

title: The relative effects of algaecides and nanobubble ozone treatment (NBOT) on nontarget zooplankton in a mesocosm study
authors: Stanislawczyk K, Braig EC, Laughinghouse HD, Raymond HA, Syed HE, Fuchs JD, Weavers LK, Chaffin JD
scale: 15 outdoor ~2,000 L mesocosm tanks at Stone Lab, Lake Erie; 5 treatments x 3 replicate tanks; Lake Erie plankton inoculum with added N and P
dose: Untreated control; SeClear copper algaecide 1 mg Cu/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 at 10 mg H2O2/L; NBOT at 0.9 and 4.6 mg O3/L
duration: Single treatment on day 8 after inoculation; zooplankton followed to 120 h
result: At 120 h total zooplankton changed +120% in controls, +90% (low NBOT) and +10% (high NBOT), but -80% (copper) and -90% (peroxide); cladocerans fell 70-100% under both algaecides. Phytoplankton declined similarly in all treatments over the first 48 h.
env_effects: Higher ozone dose reduced Bosmina, but less than the algaecides. Copper and H2O2 harmed zooplankton more than ozone nanobubbles.
key_details: Replicated mesocosm (n = 3 tanks per treatment) testing non-target effects only; the phytoplankton was mostly green algae (72.7% of chl-a; cyanobacteria 15.4%) at 30 ug/L chl-a, so it is not a test of bloom control. Differences in zooplankton were attributed to direct toxicity because phytoplankton responses were similar; chl-a in the peroxide tanks rebounded to control levels by 120 h but zooplankton did not. Calanoids and Leptodora showed no significant effects owing to low densities. Tanks were shaded ~55% and mixed twice daily.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record said duration unknown; it is 120 h after one dose. The test community was green-algae dominated, not a cyanobacterial bloom.

title: UV-C irradiation for harmful algal blooms control: A literature review on effectiveness, mechanisms, influencing factors and facilities
authors: Li S, Tao Y, Zhan XM, Dao GH, Hu HY
result: UV-C suppresses microalgal growth in proportion to dose, but sensitivity varies between species and cells can regrow through photoreactivation and dark repair. Field cases cited: a UV boat (48 mJ/cm2 killed all Peridinium bipes at <=5.0 x 10^3 cells/mL; 700 m3/h) and a boat killing 80% of Chattonella in 40 s in the Ariake Sea.
env_effects: No chemical residue, but efficacy depends on UV transmittance, salinity and pH; flow-through reactors and ship-borne units proposed for field use.
key_details: Literature review, no new experiments. Cited field tests: a 1991 Japanese mesocosm with a 30 W UV lamp removed almost all live Peridinium bipes within 2 days; a UV boat treated 2.0 x 10^4 m2 in 5 h, needing 120 mJ/cm2 for 90% kill at >1.0 x 10^4 cells/mL. The authors note most studies are static lab tests on M. aeruginosa in culture medium and call for larger field tests, multi-species work and repeated irradiation to counter regrowth. Efficacy depends on UV transmittance, salinity and pH.

title: Direct and indirect inactivation of Microcystis aeruginosa by UV-radiation
authors: Alam ZB, Otaki M, Furumai H, Ohgaki S
scale: 40 mL samples in petri dishes (0.67 cm deep), then incubated in 60 mL tubes; ~10^5 cells/mL; triplicate
dose: UV-C 254 nm at 37, 75 and 150 mW s/cm2 (1-1.5 mW/cm2 for 30 s to 2 min)
result: By day 3 all irradiated samples had <25% of the control cell density; 150 mW s/cm2 killed all cells by day 7, while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 left cells alive but not dividing for 7 days. Over 90% of cells settled within 3 days at all doses (all settled at 75 mW s/cm2).
env_effects: UV of algal extracellular products had a residual growth-control effect lasting up to 7 days; UV produced micromolar H2O2, judged too low to explain the residual effect. Framed as an alternative to non-specific copper sulfate.
key_details: Lab study with axenic M. aeruginosa (NIES) in CT medium, pH 9.0, 25 C, irradiated with low-pressure mercury lamps and incubated with unirradiated controls; growth runs in triplicate, counting only undamaged cells. Control density rose from 54 x 10^3 to 1039 x 10^3 cells/mL over 7 days while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 samples stayed flat. Separate tests showed UV-irradiated algal extracellular products had a residual growth-suppression effect and UV produced micromolar H2O2. Authors propose UV before the bloom season for small eutrophic lakes; no field test.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record says 75 mW s/cm2 was lethal; in the full text 150 mW s/cm2 was the lethal dose (all cells dead by day 7), while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 both stopped division without killing cells. The 150 dose was missing from the record.

title: Chlorination of Microcystis aeruginosa suspension: cell lysis, toxin release and degradation
authors: Ma M, Liu R, Liu H, Qu J
result: Chlorine exposure as low as 0.8 mg/L min released 63% of intracellular K+; membrane damage outpaced toxin release, and extracellular MC-LR accumulated because release was faster than degradation, peaking at 60, 30 and 1 min for 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 mg/L.
env_effects: Low chlorine doses raise dissolved microcystin; release of intracellular organic matter (a by-product precursor).

title: The effect of electrode materials on the removal of red tide organisms by microelectrolysis
authors: Wei Z, Zang X, Yu Z, Jiang K, Cao X, Song X
dose: electrolysed artificial seawater (DSA, Pt or BDD anode, Ti cathode; up to 0.75 A/cm2, 4 min) added as 250 or 500 uL aliquots to 50 mL algal suspension; 580 mg/L hypochlorite in electrolyte = 5.8 mg/L initial in the suspension
result: Best removal was 81.69 +/- 2.27% (DSA), 69.89 +/- 3.07% (Pt) and 64.43 +/- 4.10% (BDD). Hypochlorite (>95% of total chlorine) was the main algicide; H2O2 at 0.025 mg/L gave only 15% removal.
env_effects: Active oxidant is hypochlorite from seawater electrolysis; authors note chlorine can rupture Heterosigma membranes and may release intracellular toxin, and call for trials on ecological impacts. DSA used 25% and 17% less power than BDD and Pt.
key_details: Bench study with cultured Heterosigma akashiwo in L1 medium; electrolyte was produced separately and pipetted into 50 mL algal suspensions in cuvettes. Removal was estimated from in vivo fluorescence (linear with cell counts from 0.1 x 10^8 to 2.5 x 10^8 cells/L); results given as mean +/- SD. The authors cite 70-80% removal as the threshold needed in the field to stop recurrence. No field or ecological tests were done; the treatment is effectively electro-chlorination.
fulltext_discrepancy: Minor: the device does not treat algae directly by electrolysis; electrolysed seawater is dosed into the suspension (initial hypochlorite ~5.8 mg/L for >80% inactivation).

title: Photocatalytic inactivation and destruction of harmful microalgae Karenia mikimotoi under visible-light irradiation: Insights into physiological response and toxicity assessment
authors: Wang W, Liao P, Li G, Chen H, Cen J, Lu S, Wong PK, An T
scale: bench photochemical reactor; K. mikimotoi (Daya Bay strain) ~3.78 x 10^4 cells/mL
dose: 50 wt% g-C3N4/TiO2 film on FTO glass (7.065 cm2 coating) under visible light (>=420 nm)
result: Inactivation reached 64% within 60 min (in vivo chlorophyll-a fluorescence); h+ and singlet oxygen were the main reactive species and cells ruptured.
env_effects: About 71% of intracellular organic matter was released after 1 h of treatment (possible secondary pollution); acute toxicity tests showed cytotoxicity decreased significantly after treatment. Films are immobilized and reusable.
key_details: Lab study with dark control (photocatalyst without light) and light control (light without photocatalyst). Chlorophyll-a fluorescence fell in all lit systems within 10 min, but in the light-only control it recovered to the starting level after 60 min of darkness, while with the photocatalyst it did not; net inactivation was 64% in 60 min. Cell density used (3.78 x 10^4 cells/mL) was higher than typical blooms. Mechanism: h+ and singlet oxygen causing oxidative damage, antioxidant enzyme collapse and cell lysis.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record says the released organic matter had no cytotoxicity; the full text says cytotoxicity decreased significantly, while 71% of intracellular organic matter was released.

title: Photocatalytic removal of the cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7813 and four microcystins by TiO2 coated porous glass beads with UV-LED irradiation
authors: Pestana CJ, Portela Noronha J, Hui J, Edwards C, Gunaratne HQN, Irvine JTS, Robertson PKJ, Capelo-Neto J, Lawton LA
scale: Bench: 30 mL cell suspension in 40 mL bottles, triplicates, with UV-only and TiO2-without-UV controls
dose: 700 mg TiO2 (P25)-coated foamed recycled-glass beads (0.2% w/v TiO2) in mesh pods; 90-LED 365 nm panel, 2.8 umol photons m-2 s-1 (67.5 mW total output) at 100 mm; air sparged
result: Cell density fell from 15 to 10 x 10^6 cells/mL (35%) in 7 days while both controls grew to 32-34 x 10^6 cells/mL (+213-226%); intracellular microcystins fell 49% (0.69 to 0.35 ug/mL), total microcystin removal was 74%, and released microcystins were fully removed.
env_effects: Toxins released by damaged cells were destroyed by the photocatalyst; low-cost LEDs and recycled glass proposed for in-reservoir use.
key_details: Lab test with M. aeruginosa PCC7813 at a very high start density (15 x 10^6 cells/mL) in artificial freshwater. Three treatments in triplicate: TiO2 beads + UV, UV only, TiO2 beads under ambient light only; UV-only and TiO2-only controls did not differ (p > 0.05). Decline began after 48 h; biovolume was 66% of the TiO2 control. Low-energy UV-LEDs are not germicidal alone. No in-reservoir testing; the in-reservoir unit is a proposal.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record called the scale a 'prototype in-reservoir unit'; it was 30 mL bottles. The 35% is the drop from the starting density; relative to controls the treated density was about 70% lower (10 vs 32-34 x 10^6 cells/mL).

title: Control of the red tide dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides by ozone in seawater
authors: Shin M, Lee HJ, Kim MS, Park NB, Lee C
scale: 10 mL cultures in 25 mL batch flasks with natural Busan seawater; 0.5-3.0 x 10^3 cells/mL
result: Ozone inactivated 40-95% of viable C. polykrikoides within 20 s; doses >1 mg/L removed all viable cells within 300 s, and 5 mg/L destroyed all cells within 100 s. Efficacy fell with higher cell density, humic acid, pH and temperature.
env_effects: Ozonation of seawater forms HOBr and carcinogenic bromate: 0.75 ug/L BrO3- at 0.5 mg/L ozone but 278 ug/L at 5 mg/L (WHO drinking-water guideline 10 ug/L); negligible below 1 mg/L. Possible release of intracellular toxins was not tested.
key_details: Bench batch experiments with cultured C. polykrikoides (NFRDI isolate) diluted in natural seawater, dosed with ozone at several concentrations; viable (motile) and total cells counted by microscope. Inactivation was two-stage: instant kill by molecular ozone, then slow kill by residual ozone and HOBr. Over 90% of the ozone decomposed within 20 s. Bicarbonate increased efficacy and humic acid reduced it. Bromate data came from Br- spiked DI water because the method failed in seawater. No field or aquaculture-scale test.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the bromate byproduct risk (278 ug/L at 5 mg/L ozone).

title: Mote Marine's ozone experiment works, sort of, but it's not the silver bullet to kill Red Tide (with CBS News coverage of the same test)
authors: Pittman C (Tampa Bay Times); CBS News
venue: Tampa Bay Times; CBS News (press coverage)
scale: dead-end canal (Damfino Street, Boca Grande, Florida); system processes 300 gallons/min
result: Press reports only: the canal system ran five days and was described as working 'sort of' but not a silver bullet; Pierce (Mote) said it removes red tide, toxins and decomposing organic matter. No cell or toxin numbers were published.
env_effects: Researchers named the size of the treated area and performance in a natural ecosystem as the main challenges; not intended for open water. Ozonix (ozone + cavitation + electrochemical, Mote 2025) likewise has no published results.
